title: Implementation of mental health screening tools among women refugees and asylum seekers in the United States: A systematic review
content:
by Pierre J. Amiel, Shalini Suresh, Abdulaziz Almuhanna, Pratik Chhetri, John Pateña, Joyce Gyamfi, Dorice Vieira, Chukwuemeka Iloegbu, Emmanuel Peprah

Globally, displaced populations face significant mental health challenges, with women refugees and asylum seekers experiencing greater risks of anxiety, depression, and post-traumatic stress disorder. Despite the widespread use of mental health screening tools such as the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9), the Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD-7), and the Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder Checklist (PCL-5), their implementation among refugee women remains underexplored. This systematic review examines the adoption, appropriateness, acceptability, and fidelity of use of mental health screening tools for adult women refugees and asylum seekers in the United States. By identifying and synthesizing evidence on critical gaps, this study aims to inform improvements in mental health screening and care for this vulnerable population. A systematic search across ten databases identified relevant studies examining the four key implementation research outcomes (i.e., adoption, appropriateness, acceptability, and fidelity). No restrictions were applied regarding publication year or language. Screening and data extraction were conducted using Covidence, focusing on study design, relevant screening tools for common mental health disorders, and demographic details. Both quantitative and qualitative analyses were performed to synthesize the data. Our search identified 2,011 studies, from which 1,041 duplicates were removed by Covidence and an additional 49 were manually deduplicated, leaving 921 studies for screening. Ultimately, 37 studies met the inclusion criteria, however only three specifically addressed our population of interest. These reported qualitative data on appropriateness and acceptability, demonstrating positive outcomes. This systematic review underscores significant gaps in the implementation of mental health screening tools for women refugees and asylum seekers in the U.S. Data remains limited, with inconsistent reporting on key implementation research outcomes including adoption, appropriateness, acceptability, and fidelity. Our findings point to a need for research explicitly examining implementation processes and outcomes to guide evidence-based practices and ensure culturally responsive mental health care for refugee women.
